title: Why ancestry matters

blocks.what_we_do: Explain how population structure can confound an association study.
blocks.why: If case recruitment and control recruitment sample different ancestry proportions, allele frequencies can differ even at sites unrelated to disease. A principal component (PC) summarises a direction of genetic variation across many sites. Principal component analysis (PCA) describes patterns; its axes are not diagnoses, nationality or ethnicity. Reference labels are contextual metadata, not a biological ranking. We define an ancestry-matched teaching cohort before examining association p-values.
blocks.you_need: The module 4 boundary, plus the supplied GRCh38 reference subset.
blocks.command:
```{r s5-1}
reference <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "pca_reference", "ref1000g_grch38")
reference_samples <- guided_table(paste0(reference, ".psam"))
table(reference_samples$SuperPop)
```

blocks.expected_result:
This supplied subset has 1,062 samples labelled EUR, AFR, EAS and SAS. The labels describe reference sampling metadata; the table shows the groups actually present, not every possible 1000 Genomes group.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks and instructor reference counts passed on Windows.
blocks.troubleshooting: Stop at the first error. Check the named input and the previous step. Keep the command and console logs; do not substitute files from a different dataset version. See [troubleshooting](../docs/troubleshooting.md).
blocks.quick_check:
Can a disease-associated allele-frequency difference arise from unequal ancestry proportions even when a site has no disease effect?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

Yes. Ancestry can be a common cause of group membership and allele-frequency differences.

</details>
